props.text: What Lan Knew · Out March 4, 2025 · Riverhead Books
On the night her sister died, Lan Petrescu was at a wedding she had not been invited to, eating a piece of cake she had not paid for, and the woman beside her was crying about the bride.

That is the opening line of my third novel. The cake is white-almond. The wedding is in Bucharest, in 1996, in the basement of a mid-century hotel that does not exist anymore. The woman crying about the bride is not the bride's mother. The woman crying about the bride did not know there was going to be a bride at all when she walked in. None of these are the things the book is about. The thing the book is about is what Lan does the next morning, when she finally answers her phone.

content.heading: Three novels. One a year for a year, then three years apart, then two.
content.subheading: I do not write fast. I write again.

props.text: When I was 24 I worked the overnight shift at a 24-hour diner in Astoria, Queens, called the Gold Star. The cook was a man named Octavio who had been a literature professor in Bucharest before 1989 and who, on slow nights, would write the first sentences of imaginary novels on the backs of order tickets and slide them under the heat lamp for me to read. He never wrote a second sentence. He said the second sentence was where the writers gave up.

I did not understand him. I did not start writing fiction for another six years. When I did, I spent the first novel — Knife Light — trying to write a book that would have looked good to Octavio on a heat lamp. I had it in my head that every chapter needed an opening line he would not have crumpled. The book sold well enough. The PEN/Hemingway people were very kind. But the second novel was the one that taught me Octavio was wrong. The second sentence is not where writers give up. The second sentence is where writers begin.

I think about him still. He died in 2018, before the second novel came out. I dedicated The Eighth Note to him in a single line at the front of the book that no one outside my family understood. It says: For O., who only wrote the openings. The thing the dedication does not say is that his last opening was about a woman at a wedding she had not been invited to, eating a piece of cake she had not paid for. I have been writing that book for seven years. It is finally out. He cannot read it.

props.quote: The most assured American novel of the year. Chen writes the way Bucharest in 1996 actually felt — the basement weddings, the rotary phones, the cake. A masterpiece.
props.author: Parul Sehgal

props.quote: The Eighth Note refuses every easy move. I read it on a flight to São Paulo and finished it in the airport hotel before I unpacked. The dedication is one of the great dedications.
props.author: Min Jin Lee
props.role: Author of Pachinko · in praise of The Eighth Note

props.quote: The reason I keep coming back to Chen is that she does not waste a paragraph. Her openings are famous. Her endings should be too. What Lan Knew has the best ending I have read in five years.
props.author: Lauren Groff

props.title: On second-person narration, and why I will not be using it again.
props.excerpt: I wrote the second chapter of Knife Light in second person. Three readers wrote me letters about it. Two were thoughtful. One was furious. The furious one was right.

props.title: What I learned writing the same scene 14 times.
props.excerpt: The opening of What Lan Knew exists in 14 versions on my hard drive. Octavio would have crumpled 13 of them. I made him stand at my shoulder for the 14th.

props.title: On dedications no one outside the family understands.
props.excerpt: The Eighth Note is dedicated 'For O., who only wrote the openings.' I have been asked about it 200 times. This is the only place I will explain it.
